evidence.note: The 1916 film adapts William Gillette's stage play 'Sherlock Holmes,' first commercially published in authorized text form by Doubleday in 1922 â€” within the pre-1930 bright line. The play itself was based on Conan Doyle's stories: 'A Scandal in Bohemia' (US book publication 1892), 'The Final Problem' (1894), and A Study in Scarlet (1887 UK, 1890 US). editorial:
The 1916 Essanay production is the only known filmed record of William Gillette performing the Holmes role he had made canonical across more than 1,300 stage appearances since 1899. Directed by Arthur Berthelet in Essanay's Chicago studios and released May 15, 1916, the seven-reel silent feature stars a 63-year-old Gillette opposite Edward Fielding as Watson and Ernest Maupain as Moriarty, adapting Gillette's own 1899 stage play â€” which Conan Doyle personally endorsed â€” and drawing on 'A Scandal in Bohemia,' 'The Final Problem,' and A Study in Scarlet. Every print was assumed destroyed until October 2014, when a nitrate negative bearing French-language intertitles surfaced at the CinÃ©mathÃ¨que franÃ§aise; the San Francisco Silent Film Festival restored it from the 35mm source and premiered the recovered film in 2015 with live accompaniment by the Donald Sosin Ensemble.

For a creator sourcing public-domain footage, the image track is clean: Essanay's 1916 copyright lapsed no later than 1944, Essanay itself had dissolved before any renewal could be filed, and both the underlying Doyle stories and Gillette's 1922 published play text fall squarely under the pre-1930 bright line. The operative rights trap is the 2015 SFSFF restoration. The restoration masters are a post-1978 copyrighted work owned by the San Francisco Silent Film Festival, and the Donald Sosin Ensemble's accompaniment adds a second protected layer. The community uploads on Archive.org (identifiers SherlockHolmes1916 and sherlock-holmes-1916) circulate without the Sosin score and are safe to reuse; anyone wanting the polished 2015 theatrical version should contact SFSFF before any commercial application.
faq: Is the 1916 Sherlock Holmes film truly in the public domain despite the Conan Doyle estate's history of asserting rights?

Yes. Essanay released the film on May 15, 1916, and the 28-year initial copyright term expired no later than 1944. Essanay dissolved around 1918, leaving no successor to file a renewal, and no renewal record has been located. The estate's legal assertions â€” including the Klinger litigation decided by the 7th Circuit in 2014 â€” were copyright-based claims on Doyle's stories, not claims on this film's lapsed copyright. The pre-1930 bright-line rule makes this a settled call: the images are public domain in the United States.
Can I use the restored version available on the Internet Archive?

The community uploads (archive.org/details/SherlockHolmes1916 and archive.org/details/sherlock-holmes-1916) are public-domain copies of the footage and are free to use. The 2015 SFSFF theatrical restoration is a different matter: its digital restoration masters and the Donald Sosin Ensemble score are post-1978 copyrights owned by the San Francisco Silent Film Festival. If the version you are using credits SFSFF or carries the Sosin accompaniment, seek clearance from SFSFF before commercial use.
